The Mezze Table: A Spread That Doesn’t Need a Centerpiece

by Karen Tedesco — August 6, 2026
See Recipe

This post may contain affiliate links. Please read my disclosure policy.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:48
Instaread

Most entertaining advice centers on one big thing — a whole roasted chicken, a showstopper cake, the dish everyone’s supposed to remember. Mezze plates reject that idea entirely. It’s a spread composed of several smaller dishes, each pulling its own weight, with nothing standing at the center demanding attention.

What I love about a table or kitchen island set up this way is watching what happens around it — people reaching across each other, talking with their mouths full, going back for more of the thing they didn’t expect to like.

I started creating tables like this back when I threw dinner parties as a personal chef — they can be the warm-up that happens before a meal really gets going, or sometimes the entire menu.

What to add to the platter

These aren’t strict categories so much as a checklist for you to keep balance in mind — a lot like putting together a cheese plate, where you want one creamy, one aged, one blue, rather than three of the same thing. A platter with three dips and nothing else will feel monotonous; one with too many competing textures starts to feel chaotic. I start from a short list — something creamy like whipped hummus or baba ganoush, something with bite, something warm, something raw — and let whichever recipes are already in my fridge fill them in.

Herb Hummus — Ultra-Creamy Whipped Chickpeas

This is the hummus that ruins store-bought versions for you (maybe forever) — whipped up with a generous amount of tahini and a full cup of fresh herbs, so it's more green than beige. Give the food processor its full three minutes and don't rush the process — that's the whole secret.
Get the Recipe

Muhammara Recipe

My everyday muhammara — toasted walnuts and roasted red peppers blended with pomegranate molasses for a dip that's smoky, a little sweet, and a little tangy all at once. Set it out on a mezze platter, spread it on sandwiches, or spoon it over grilled chicken or fish.
Get the Recipe

Oven-Roasted Baba Ganoush

You don't need to fire up the grill to make baba ganoush. My version tastes a little smoky, a little spicy, and perfectly tangy — mash it coarse or blend it silky just the way you enjoy it.
Get the Recipe

Roasted Red Pepper Romesco Sauce (No Nuts)

A quick, no-nuts version of romesco — the roasted peppers alone give it all the body it needs. Ready in about 20 minutes, and it keeps in the fridge for whatever you want to spoon it over next.
Get the Recipe

Vegetable Tabbouleh Bulgur Salad

Whole wheat bulgur, chickpeas, crisp vegetables and fresh herbs layered in a creamy tahini dressing spiked with cumin and red pepper. Substantial enough to serve as a main dish, and the flavors get even better overnight.
Get the Recipe

Spiced Chickpea Salad with Tahini and Pita Crunch

A riff on a simple Middle Eastern garbanzo salad — falafel spices warmed in olive oil, a tangy tahini dressing, and crushed pita chips for unexpected crunch
Get the Recipe

Baked Feta Shrimp and Tomatoes

A delicious one-dish dinner: Garlicky baked shrimp and feta with juicy cherry tomatoes and herbs. This recipe is ready in 30 minutes and couldn't be simpler!
Get the Recipe

Baked Ratatouille with Goat Cheese and Pesto

Classic Provençal ratatouille, made a little easier — combine roughly chopped summer vegetables and roast until caramelized and jammy. Finish the dish with crumbled goat cheese and a swirl of basil pesto while everything is still steaming hot.
Get the Recipe

What to do with the leftovers

Once a platter’s been out for a few hours with people’s hands in and out of it, the dips themselves are done — and they aren’t safe to save, no matter how good the muhammara still looks. Toss them into the trash.

The raw vegetables are a different story. Odd ends of carrot, cucumber, celery, or fennel that never made it onto anyone’s plate can go straight into a bag in the freezer for the next time you make chicken broth or soup — no need for them to go to waste just because the party’s over, and cooking will eliminate any issues.

And any bread or pita that’s gone stale is exactly what you want for homemade breadcrumbs — better texture and flavor than a store-bought box, and one less thing headed for the trash.

A Mezze Platter for 8

Karen Tedesco
Several small dishes — a dip, a salad, something warm from the oven — arranged so nothing has to carry the whole meal. This is the mezze platter I put together when nothing needs a centerpiece and small plates are the whole point of having people over.
Print Recipe Pin Recipe Leave a Review
Yield: 8 servings
Prep Time: 15 minutes mins
Cook Time: 0 minutes mins
Total Time: 15 minutes mins

Ingredients
 

2-3 dips, such as:

  • Creamy Herb Hummus
  • Muhammara
  • Smoky Baba Ganoush
  • Roasted Red Pepper Romesco

1 hearty salad with texture

  • Vegetable Tabbouleh Salad
  • Pita Crunch Chickpea Salad

Something warm or baked

  • Feta Shrimp with Tomatoes
  • No-Fuss Roasted Ratatouille

Crisp raw vegetables

  • Sliced seedless cucumbers, carrots, radishes

1-2 briny items

  • Feta cheese chunks drizzled with olive oil
  • Olives (I like to briefly warm them in a microwave or on top of the stove, with a drizzle of olive oil)

The finishing touches

  • Assortment of seeded crackers, warm pita or flatbread
  • Olive oil and flaky salt

Equipment

  • 14-15-inch serving platter or large board

Instructions
 

  1. Start with the dips in the center — spoon them into bowls or spread them straight onto the platter in swoops using the back of a large spoon.
  2. Arrange the salads in medium bowls around the dips, leaving room to breathe between them. Serve the baked dish in its own dish, set on top of a trivet.
  3. Fill the gaps with raw vegetables, bread, and small bowls of feta cheese and pickled things
  4. Finish with a drizzle of olive oil over the dips and a scatter of flaky salt right before serving.

Notes

  • For a vegetarian platter, skip the feta shrimp and stick with the ratatouille and dips.
  • Most of the dips keep 4–5 days in the fridge on their own, but assemble the platter itself no more than an hour before serving so the raw vegetables stay crisp.
